items.headline: Foundational raises £8.2M to commercialize satellite laser ranging
items.title: Foundational Raises £8.2M for Satellite Laser Ranging
items.scifi_hook: A London startup will bounce lasers off orbiting mirrors to measure satellite positions with pencil‑thin precision.
items.eli5: They fire lasers at reflectors on satellites and time the return to know exact distances.
items.why: Precise tracking improves navigation, climate data and space traffic safety.
items.text: Foundational wants to turn bouncing lasers off satellites into a commercial service. The London startup emerged from stealth today with an £8.2M ($10.8M) pre-seed round—which it says is Europe’s largest space-tech pre-seed to date. Investors include early-stage VC firms Inflection, BACKED, and Adjacent, alongside Type One Ventures and Final Frontier, a European fund focused on defense, space, and cyber. Origin story: Foundational CEO Hira Virdee founded SSA data company Lumi Space in 2018, which was focused on pure R&D and government projects. Last year, he partnered with CTO Dave Gooding to cofound Foundational to commercialize the tech, bringing Lumi in as a subsidiary. “From the company formation to landing the term sheet and closing the investment was very, very quick,” Virdee told Payload. “I think a lot of that was testament to the previous work.” Mirror, mirror: Foundational is automating and scaling satellite laser ranging (SLR), a highly precise method for measuring the distance to satellites. The company likens its accuracy to detecting a car in Edinburgh rolling forward by the width of a pencil—from a viewpoint in London. Its system combines three pieces: Retroreflectors on satellites, which keep working even after a satellite dies; Automated ground stations that fire laser pulses at them and time the light’s return; A software platform that processes and delivers the data. SLR dates back to the 1960s, but legacy stations are expensive and require staff. Foundation

items.headline: DOE funds $29.5M for 17 national‑lab mining‑tech projects
items.title: US DOE awards $29.5M for 17 National Lab mining tech projects
items.scifi_hook: U.S. labs will field‑test autonomous robots and electric extraction tools to mine critical minerals at scale.
items.eli5: The Energy Department is paying labs to turn lab‑scale mining ideas into real‑world machines.
items.why: Advances aim to cut reliance on foreign critical‑metal supplies.
items.text: The US Department of Energy announced Wednesday $29.5 million for 17 mining technology projects across 12 National Laboratories through the Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation’s (CMEI) Mine of the Future Initiative. The projects, DOE said, will reduce dependence on foreign supply chains, bolster national security, and advance the technologies that will establish America’s long‑term energy independence. They are focused on moving next-generation mining, extraction, and processing technologies from the laboratory toward field testing and commercial deployment. Applications span underground recovery, autonomous exploration, secondary sourcing, and advanced beneficiation. Underground recovery Five projects are advancing in-situ extraction technologies, including electric-hydraulic fracturing at Idaho National Laboratory to low-voltage lithium extraction from clay at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Oak Ridge National Laboratory is developing a mobile rvgdeobotics platform designed to map underground mines and identify mineral deposits in minutes rather than weeks. Mine waste and secondary sourcing Argonne National Laboratory is working on recovery of copper, nickel, and cobalt from mine tailings, while SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory is developing technology to extract vanadium from aging oil and gas infrastructure. items.headline: Researchers propose global tax framework for future space mining
items.title: Space miners may face an Earth-sized tax problem
items.scifi_hook: A new model suggests a UN‑run tax on lunar and asteroid ore, sharing revenue with all nations.
items.eli5: They suggest a worldwide system to tax space‑mined resources and give part of the money to countries without space programs.
items.why: A clear tax regime could enable sustainable commercial space mining.
items.text: Miners may one day extract fortunes from the Moon and asteroids, but governments will have to figure out how to take their cut without killing the industry before it gets off the ground. Research co-authored by Petr Zimčík, head of the Center for Economics and Data Analytics at NEWTON University, proposes a system that would account for inflation, exchange-rate movements and commodity-price volatility while distributing some revenue to countries without space-mining capabilities. “The best approach is to divide overall space mining tax revenues for two different purposes,” Zimčík told MINING.COM. “The first is to create a Global Space Resource Dividend for countries.” The framework seeks to address questions governments may eventually face as companies move closer to extracting resources from the Moon, asteroids and other celestial bodies: who collects taxes, when they become payable, how resources without market prices are valued and whether countries lacking space technology should share in the proceeds. Taxing space Zimčík said a central tax authority could be established through a multilateral treaty negotiated under the United Nations, following a process similar to the development of the Outer Space Treaty in the 1960s. items.headline: DoD awards Texas startup contract to recover scandium from waste
items.title: Texas startup awarded DoD contract for scandium recovery
items.scifi_hook: A university spin‑out will extract rare‑earth scandium from American industrial by‑products for defense use.
items.eli5: The startup uses chemistry to pull scandium out of waste streams, a metal the U.S. currently imports.
items.why: Domestic scandium supply could strengthen aerospace and energy tech independence.
items.text: Technology startup Supra Elemental Recovery announced Wednesday that the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) Defense Logistics Agency has awarded it a Phase I Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) contract to advance recovery of scandium. The company didn’t disclose the amount of the award. The contract, it said, will bolster Supra’s recovery of rare earth elements from North American industrial byproducts. Spun out of the University of Texas at Austin, Supra recovers and refines critical minerals using peer-reviewed separation technologies at mining and industrial site. Supra’s proprietary platform utilizes advanced chemical separation technology to selectively recover target elements from industrial feedstocks. Under the SBIR, Supra will evaluate the feasibility of applying its separation platform to relevant feedstocks in support of potential future scalability. Scandium is a key mineral utilized in advanced aerospace, energy, and commercial technologies. There is currently no commercial scandium mining or production in the United States, and the country relies entirely on imports from foreign markets. The research effort aims to evaluate novel separation and processing technologies to support domestic supply chain diversity. “The U.S. has scandium resources onshore,” Supra CEO Katie Durham said in a news release . “Our technology is built to recover this scandium at high purity and at scale to meet domestic demand.”
